titulo: Much, many, a few, a little
titulo_es: Quantifiers: much, many, a few, a little
descripcion_es: Expressing quantity with countable and uncountable nouns.
resumen: The choice of quantifier depends on whether the noun is countable (books, people) or uncountable (water, money, information). Many and a few go with countable nouns; much and a little, with uncountable nouns.

filas: some, a small amount (positive idea) (es: algunos, un poco)
not many, not much (negative idea) (es: pocos, poco)

explicacion.texto: Much and many are used mainly in questions and negative sentences (I don't have much time; Are there many people?). In affirmative sentences a lot of sounds more natural (We have a lot of work).

A few / a little mean “some, a small amount” and have a positive meaning: I have a few friends here (I have some friends). Without a, few / little stress that the amount is not enough: Few people came (not many people came).

items: Common nouns that are uncountable in English but countable in Spanish: information, advice, news, furniture, luggage, homework, research, equipment.
They take no -s and no a / an: some advice, a piece of advice.
Too much / too many = more than is wanted or needed: There are too many cars.

ejemplos.frase: How many brothers and sisters have you got?
There are a few apples in the fridge.
ejemplos.traduccion: Hay unas cuantas manzanas en la nevera.

ejemplos.frase: Could I have a little sugar, please?
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Me pones un poco de azúcar, por favor?

ejemplos.frase: She gave me some good advice.
Very few students passed the exam.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: People is a countable plural noun: many.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Can you give me some informations?
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Can you give me some information?

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I have a little friends in London.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I have a few friends in London.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With countable plural nouns, use a few.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the table in Rules and key points that separates countable and uncountable nouns: to ask about quantity with an uncountable noun, you use How much. The clue is money, which is uncountable in English: it never takes -s and you never say a money, even though we count euros. That is why the correct question is How much money do you need?, with much before a noun without a plural.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Many only goes with countable plural nouns (many coins, many euros). Money is uncountable, so it requires much.
You must choose just one form; money is uncountable and only allows much.

ejercicios.frase: There aren't ___ hotels in this village.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule is the one in the table: a large quantity with countable plural nouns is many. The clue is hotels, a countable noun with a plural -s. In addition, the sentence is negative (aren't), which is exactly the context where many sounds natural according to the card; in affirmative sentences a lot of is preferred. Therefore: There aren't many hotels.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hay muchos hoteles en este pueblo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Much goes with uncountable nouns (much time, much money). Hotels is countable plural, so it needs many.
Of would be missing (a lot of hotels), and besides, the exercise asks you to choose between much and many.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a few or a little.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row of the table “some, a small amount (positive idea)”: with uncountable nouns you use a little. Salt is uncountable (we do not say two salts), and the idea is positive: adding a small amount. That is why Add a little salt. A few could only go with something countable, such as a few drops.
ejercicios.traduccion: Añade un poco de sal al agua.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A few goes with countable plural nouns (a few eggs). Salt is uncountable, so you need a little.
Without a, little means “not much, not enough” and has a negative meaning; here the instruction asks you to add some salt, a positive idea: a little.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a few or a little.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule is the one for a few / a little: a few goes with countable plural nouns and has a positive meaning (“some”). The clue is minutes, countable and plural. The sentence expresses a small but sufficient quantity, without complaint, so the correct form is a few minutes.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Minutes is countable plural: a few.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A little goes with uncountable nouns (a little time). Minutes is countable plural and needs a few.
Without a, few means “not many, not enough”; here there is no negative idea, just a small quantity: a few.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the list in Rules and key points of nouns that are uncountable in English but countable in Spanish: homework is uncountable in English. Although in Spanish we say “muchos deberes”, homeworks does not exist in English, so the negative sentence takes much: We didn't have much homework. If you want to count, you say a piece of homework or two exercises.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Homework is uncountable in English: much.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It copies the Spanish “muchos deberes”. Homework is uncountable in English and only allows much.
Homework has no plural in English and the gap only needs the quantifier; the correct form is much.

ejercicios.frase: There are too ___ chairs in this room.
ejercicios.explicacion: The list on the card reminds you that too much / too many mean “more than is wanted or needed”, and that the choice depends on the noun. Chairs is countable and plural, and the verb are confirms it. That is why the only correct option is too many chairs.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Chairs is countable plural: too many.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay demasiadas sillas en esta habitación.

por_opcion.much: Incorrect: too much goes with uncountable nouns (too much noise). Chairs is countable plural.
por_opcion.many: Correct: too many + countable plural noun means “more than wanted or needed”.
por_opcion.little: Incorrect: too little means “not enough” and goes with uncountable nouns (too little time); with chairs it fits neither in form nor in meaning.

ejercicios.frase: The town is very quiet. ___ tourists visit it.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for few / little without a: they stress that the quantity is small, with a negative meaning. The clue is the previous sentence: the village is very quiet, so not many tourists come. Tourists is countable plural, so few is the right choice, not little. Few tourists visit it = not many tourists visit it.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Countable plural with a negative meaning (not many): few.
ejercicios.traduccion: El pueblo es muy tranquilo. Pocos turistas lo visitan.

por_opcion.Few: Correct: few + countable plural expresses “not many”, with an idea of scarcity, which is what the context requires.
por_opcion.Little: Incorrect: little is the equivalent for uncountable nouns (little traffic). Tourists is countable.
por_opcion.Much: Incorrect: much goes with uncountable nouns and, besides, it would mean “a lot”, the opposite of what a quiet village suggests.

ejercicios.frase: Can I ask you for some ___?
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the card's list of uncountable nouns: advice is uncountable in English, so it takes no -s and no a / an. The clue is some, which with uncountable nouns means “a certain amount of”. In Spanish we say “un consejo” or “unos consejos”, but in English you say some advice or, to count, a piece of advice.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Advice is uncountable: no -s and no an.

por_opcion.advices: Incorrect: advice has no plural in English; advices is a literal copy of the Spanish “consejos”.
por_opcion.advice: Correct: some advice is the normal way to ask for advice, because advice is uncountable.
por_opcion.an advice: Incorrect: an uncountable noun does not take a / an. For the Spanish “un consejo” you say a piece of advice.

ejercicios.frase: We've got ___ milk left, so we don't need to buy any.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule is the one for a little with uncountable nouns and a positive meaning. Milk is uncountable, and the second part of the sentence (we do not need to buy any) shows that the quantity is sufficient, a positive idea. That is why We've got a little milk left.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Milk is uncountable and the idea is positive (enough): a little.
ejercicios.traduccion: Nos queda un poco de leche, así que no hace falta comprar.

por_opcion.a little: Correct: uncountable (milk) and the positive meaning of “some, enough”.
por_opcion.a few: Incorrect: a few goes with countable plural nouns (a few bottles). Milk is uncountable.
por_opcion.many: Incorrect: many goes with countable plural nouns; with milk it would be much, and in an affirmative sentence a lot of would be preferred.

ejercicios.frase: How many luggage have you got?
respuestas: How much luggage have you got?
ejercicios.explicacion: The card includes luggage among the uncountable nouns that seem countable to Spanish speakers. Although we may think of suitcases (es: “maletas”), luggage is an uncountable mass noun, just like the Spanish “equipaje”, and it has no plural. That is why the question must be How much luggage have you got? If we want to count, we change the word: How many suitcases / bags?

errores_previstos.respuesta: How many luggage have you got?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: luggage is uncountable and needs much, not many.

errores_previstos.respuesta: How many luggages have you got?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Luggage does not take -s. The underlying mistake remains: with an uncountable noun you ask How much.

ejercicios.frase: I have a little questions for you.
respuestas: I have a few questions for you.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for a few / a little: with countable plural nouns you use a few. Questions is countable (one question, two questions) and plural, so a little does not work. It is the same mistake that the card lists in “I have a little friends”: the correct form is I have a few questions.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Questions is countable plural: a few.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tengo unas cuantas preguntas para ti.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have a little questions for you.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: a little only goes with uncountable nouns; questions needs a few.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have a little question for you.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Here little becomes an adjective (“a small question”), which changes the sentence and does not correct the quantifier mistake; the answer required was a few questions.

ejercicios.explicacion: Furniture appears in the card's list of uncountable nouns: in English it refers to furniture as a whole and never takes -s. Some with an uncountable noun means “a certain amount of”, so the correct sentence is They bought some new furniture. To count, you say a piece of furniture or two pieces of furniture.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: furnitures does not exist because furniture is uncountable.
An uncountable noun does not take a; for a single item you say a piece of furniture.

ejercicios.enunciado: Turn the sentence into a question about quantity with How many or How much.
ejercicios.frase: She drinks a lot of water.
respuestas: How much water does she drink?
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “what quantity?” in the table: with uncountable nouns, How much. Water is uncountable, so the question begins with How much water. Then, as it is present simple with she, you need the auxiliary does and the infinitive without -s: does she drink.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Water is uncountable: How much + does + subject + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: How many water does she drink?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Water is uncountable: the question takes How much, not How many.
A literal copy of the Spanish: the auxiliary does is missing, and it is essential in present simple questions.

errores_previstos.respuesta: How much water does she drinks?
errores_previstos.explicacion: With does, the verb goes back to the infinitive without -s: does she drink.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the words in order to make a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule is How many + countable plural noun. People is plural (the singular is person), so it needs many. In a question with there is / there are, the verb goes before there: How many people are there? The order is quantifier, noun, verb and there.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: How many + plural noun + are there.

errores_previstos.explicacion: That is the order of an indirect question (I don't know how many people there are); in a direct question, are goes before there.
A literal copy of the Spanish “¿cuántas hay personas?”: the noun goes right after How many.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that much is used mainly in negative sentences and questions, and always with uncountable nouns. Time, in the sense of duration, is uncountable, and the sentence is negative. The order is subject + don't + have + much time.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Much is used with uncountable nouns in negative sentences.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The auxiliary don't goes before the main verb: We don't have.
That would be a negative question, not the statement the exercise asks for.

descripcion_larga_es: The quantifiers much, many, a few, a little, few and little express quantity, and the choice depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable in English. It is a basic but tricky point for Spanish speakers, because words such as information, advice, news or furniture are uncountable in English even though they are counted in Spanish, and because a few and few do not mean the same thing.

contexto.que_es: They are words that go before a noun to indicate quantity: a lot, not much, some, how much. English has different forms depending on whether the noun is countable (it can be counted: one book, two books) or uncountable (it takes no plural and no a: water, money, information).
contexto.por_que_importa: They are used constantly when asking for something, asking about prices or quantities and describing situations. A mistake such as “How much people” or “some informations” is noticed immediately and gives an impression of a low level, although it rarely prevents understanding. In written exams it is a classic in gap-fill and error-correction exercises.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Whenever you talk about quantity: in questions (How much…? How many…?), negative sentences (I don't have much time) and to qualify (a few minutes, a little sugar). The clue is always the noun: if it has a plural in -s, many or a few; if it does not, much or a little. Spanish speakers tend to follow Spanish and make nouns that are uncountable in English plural.
